newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Angry Guatemala begins burial of 82 soccer dead.
newsitem.headline: Angry Guatemala begins burial of 82 soccer dead.

text.p: Angry and confused over the cause of their worst-ever sports disaster, Guatemalans on Friday began burial rites for the first of up to 82 soccer fans crushed by an avalanche of bodies at a World Cup qualifier.

Convoys of black hearses ferried trampled bodies in tin coffins from the morgue to funeral parlours within and outside the capital as the nation suffered what President Alvaro Arzu described as a "tragedy of unimaginable dimensions."

In a nationwide broadcast late on Thursday, Arzu named a high level commission to investigate the crush at the national soccer stadium during a match between Guatemala and Costa Rica on Wednesday night. He said it would report back in 15 days.
Mourning relatives and friends, many sobbing into each other's arms, lined up to pay respects to the dead at wakes in which sometimes several brothers lay side-by-side in coffins.

The exact death toll was still unclear. Interior Minister Rodolfo Mendoza said 80 people, all Guatemalans, died, but morgue officials said they received 78 corpses and another four died in hospitals. At least 147 people were injured in the worst soccer stadium disaster in World Cup history.
Amid the grief, there was outrage at the slapdash security at the match, and witnesses and government officials gave conflicting accounts of events leading up to the deaths.

Mendoza said a brawl by unruly fans in the terraces, or bleachers, was the trigger, but officials have also acknowledged there was widespread sale of forged tickets and that the 47,000-capacity stadium was overcrowded.
Witnesses said gate-crashers pushing through an entrance at the top of the stadium overwhelmed fans below, causing a mass of people to tumble down on top of each other toward the playing field.
The entrance was at street level, with the playing fields and lower stands carved into a hill. Many died crushed against a chainlink fence separating the stands from the playing field.

"The authorities were irresponsible, there's no doubt about it. At these games there is no security," said Anibal Pinon, 24, who mourned overnight in a Guatemala City funeral home for his two boyhood friends, brothers Carlos and Byron Barros.

In his first public address since he made a grief-choked appearance at the Mateo Flores stadium on Wednesday night, Arzu acknowledged problems needed to be dealt with and he appealed for national unity during the time of crisis.
"We are investigating to be able to say exactly what happened and what were the facts so that we can learn from this painful experience," he said in a broadcast preceded by a solemn funeral march.
He announced that turnstile takings from the $7-a-head match would be seized and offered as compensation to victims' families, most of which are poor.

In the small city of Mixco, 15 miles 25 km southwest of Guatemala City, more than 1,500 mourners gathered in drizzling rain to pass by the coffins of four siblings of a family of 12 and their teenage niece, trampled underfoot in the crush.
Many placed funeral donations into large tin cans on top of the coffins.
Crowd control at the wake was almost as chaotic as security at a soccer match. Pushing and shoving, many of the mourners ignored pleas from organisers to get in line.
In Guatemala City, officials said the main cemetery was booked up for back-to-back funerals all day on Friday.
In a nationwide display of grief, flags flew at half-mast and government buildings were decked with large black ribbons.
After suspending the game on Wednesday, Arzu declared three days of national mourning and followed it up with a two-day ban on sports activities.
Guatemala's soccer authorities faced possible sanctions from FIFA, world soccer's governing body, and were expecting to hear word by late Friday.

The 40-year-old stadium where tragedy struck always fills with feverish crowds during big games. In Guatemala, as elsewhere in Central America, fanatical team followers sometimes urinate in cups that they throw on those below in one of the more outrageous of soccer's bizarre rituals.
